articles.title: How to face the end of the world – according to Plato and the Stoics
articles.summary: Fearing future catastrophe is nothing new – ancient Greek and Roman philosophers all visualized the apocalypse. Do your feelings of existential dread extend beyond your own personal mortality?
body: Apocalyptic expectations are on the rise. According to a 2022 Pew Research Center survey, 39% of Americans believe that we are living in the end times.

Yet the feeling that the world is coming to an end is nothing new. Anticipating and preparing for the end of the world is an ancient practice. In fact, many of the ways in which we envision future catastrophes can be traced back to the ancient Mediterranean world.

Greek and Roman authors set up their accounts of the end of the world as the product of reason rather than divine revelation – the product of the rational study of the laws of nature that govern the universe. They saw the end of the world as an inevitability and typically saw the aftermath, if there was one, as a repeat of the cycle of human development. The main piece of wisdom they seek to provide is how to face catastrophe without fear.

This is particularly true of the Epicureans and Stoics. Their goal is to meet all events up to and including the end of the world with equanimity. The Roman poet Horace offers a summation of this ideal in his Odes: the “righteous and resolute man” will remain “undaunted even if the sky should fall and the ruins strike his head”.
points: Fearing future catastrophe is nothing new – ancient Greek and Roman philosophers all visualized the apocalypse.

articles.title: A financially comfortable friend has set up a GoFundMe for vet bills. Is this socially acceptable? | Leading questions
articles.summary: Your friends may have had good intentions when making this request, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But that needn’t dictate how you feel about it. A friend, who I believe is financially comfortable, set up a GoFundMe page to pay for vet bills for their sick dog while on holiday…
body: The family appears to be financially comfortable; both adults have good jobs, own two cars, have all the latest gadgets like expensive bikes and sporting equipment, take an annual holiday overseas and domestic holidays throughout the year, and live in a big house in a well-to-do area.
Is it socially acceptable to ask for money publicly in these circumstances?

Eleanor says: I’ll never forget someone posting their household expenses as proof it’s hard to get by on two six-figure incomes. By the time they’d paid for holidays, two cars, private school fees, insurance, extracurriculars, the mortgage and savings, there was nothing left!

They really did think this was proof they weren’t well-off. I suppose in some sense they’re right. Once you use your money to secure your financial future and have a high quality of life, you don’t have a Scrooge McDuck pile left over.

articles.title: Who needs sleep when you can scroll through home makeover videos instead | Bim Adewunmi
articles.summary: I’m not talking about frenetic whole-house renovations and stripping wallpaper but the slow, thoughtful design tweaks that are perfect for bedtime viewing. I have been doing more than my fair share of revenge bedtime procrastination.
body: I am drawn more and more to the slower projects. People who take years to redo their entire house, and then walk me through each and every design decision. This is what our parents and grandparents did, no? The homes so many of us grew up in were not subject to annual refreshing – who had the time or will to strip all that wallpaper? Not my mum! And we were no poorer for it.

One of my faves is Medina Grillo. She and her family were long-term renters until they recently bought their own home, and I adore how she makes room for trial and error. Her design choices always charm me (I’ve copied her idea of turning dish racks into book and vinyl shelving), and she is so calm and chill.

I also follow Anna Stephens on TikTok. She has a series called “three tweaks per week”, in which she undertakes three little projects and slowly shifts the vibe of her home. It has been almost a year of the videos, and I’m not sick of them yet. It’s such a simple, no-pressure idea. An ideal bedtime scroll destination.

articles.title: Has Substitution Culture Gone Too Far?
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. When Chanita Chayaluk decided to open her restaurant and wine bar Taan, she hoped “to showcase Thai food in Chicago in a different…
body: Guests are increasingly asking for their meals to be customized. These restaurants say it’s gone too far.

Another quirk of operating in Chicago? “We’re still pretty ‘Midwest nice,’” says Chayaluk. “We try to overaccommodate and appease the masses.” In the early days of service, guests made frequent requests for substitutions or accommodations due to preferences and dietary restrictions. “It would slow down service and speed, and that was not just affecting us, but the guest experience in many ways,” she says. With a small kitchen and staff, it was hard to keep up. “It just felt like we were Chipotle.” When a guest asked for green curry mussels “but without the mussels,” it was a turning point.

Chayaluk implemented a limited substitution policy at Taan, stating on Instagram that ingredients like fish sauce and shrimp paste are “the fabric that defines our cuisine,” and therefore, could not be removed from any dishes that include it.
At the same time, restaurants like Taan and New York’s Ha’s Snack Bar —which proudly announces in its Instagram bio that everything contains fish sauce—are standing their ground.
points: Guests are increasingly asking for their meals to be customized.

articles.title: Fifi's Wig Shop Brings Halloween Transformations to the Next Level
articles.summary: Fifi's Wig Shop is a must-stop destinations for elaborate, one-of-a-kind wigs. “In New Orleans, we will always find an excuse to wear a wig.”
body: It makes sense that New Orleans is a hot destination to celebrate Halloween. From the spooky ghost tours to the haunted hotels, the Louisiana city is a prime spot for getting into the macabre spirit. It’s unsurprising, then, that it’s also the best place to find one-of-a-kind costumes, too—and if you so happen to be still in need of an over-the-top wig this Halloween, there’s one particular shop that draws in both locals and tourists alike. Meet Fifi’s Custom Wigs.

The French Quarter wig shop was founded in 1977 by Marcy Hesseling, eventually taken over by Thomas O’Donnell and his husband Neil Ard back in 2023. The couple had just relocated from New York City—where O’Donnell worked in theater, and Ard in fashion—and both saw opportunity as a natural next step for their combined careers.

“I'd taken a part-time job at Fifi's, just for fun,” says O’Donnell. “Then Marcy Willy Wonka-ed us. We bought the business with the intent of carrying the torch for the foreseeable future, and so far, so good!”

articles.title: Is it Safe to Travel to Paris Right Now Amidst the France Protests?
articles.summary: As France protests and unrest continue unfolding across the capital, we share practical advice on where to stay, what to avoid, and how to navigate the city safely.
body: If there is one thing that the French know how to do, it is fight for their rights. It’s not for the goodness of politicians' hearts that university fees in France are still $200 for a bachelor's degree but thanks to a population that refuses to back down when their rights are being threatened.

Since September, French high school students have been protesting for better conditions, especially in suburban areas often forgotten by institutions. The movement has reached almost unprecedented proportions, with other sectors joining the students, demanding better learning conditions and fighting against the cost-of-living crisis, hike in fuel prices, and erosion of social welfare.

I have seen many large-scale gatherings during my years in France, but nothing like what’s unfolding right now. It’s important, however, to distinguish between peaceful demonstrators and those involved in vandalism, violence, or looting. Although not always of this magnitude, violence and looting have also marred some previous France protests, whether it’s the country winning a football match or students fighting for their rights. If you're visiting Paris soon or planning an upcoming trip, here's what to know.

articles.title: Cosplaying as a Tech Billionaire on a Caribbean Yacht
articles.summary: On a weeklong cruise, my son and I traded mega-ship buffets for locally sourced feasts, elegant plant-based dining, and midnight nachos and burgers.
body: With Hotels With Great Taste, we’re pulling back the curtain for a peek at the “special sauce” that hotels use to create memorable, meaningful culinary experiences for their guests.
If your idea of cruise ship dining is an all-night nacho bar and unlimited soft-serve, you are not alone. You’re also not entirely wrong.

The good news: Some ships are moving away from buffets with warming stations, revamping their food and beverage offerings to appeal to contemporary palates. For instance, larger cruise lines are creating onboard restaurants designed and run by Michelin-starred chefs, like Massimiliano Alajmo’s Osteria d’Ovidio aboard the Crystal Serenity. There is a focus on chic venues serving exquisite plates created à la minute, quality over quantity. Most ships cater to individual dietary needs and vibes: teens craving midnight burgers, vegan diets, gluten-free restrictions.

articles.title: The Bride Wore Handmade Silk Organza Flowers in Her Hair for Her Creative Wedding in Marrakech
articles.summary: Film director Pam Nasr tapped her friends to help design all four of her bridal looks, including her ceremony gown by Christopher John Rogers, which she paired with a chrysanthemum headpiece crafted in silk satin organza.
body: When film director Pam Nasr and Mateo de la Torre got engaged in November 2025, it was in cinematic fashion. The couple was visiting Mateo’s family for Thanksgiving on Oahu, where he grew up. “He took me on a surprise trip to Kaua’i,” Pam says, “and proposed to me in the middle of the ocean off the Nā Pali Coast.” The couple had met three years prior on Hinge. “He was the only person I spoke to and met with on the app, and we didn’t stop talking after our first date.”

As someone who works in a creative field, Pam counts several artists and designers as dear friends. So when she and Mateo began planning their wedding, it was only natural that she collaborated with these loved ones for each of her looks.

Prior to their June wedding at Ksar Char-Bagh in Marrakech, the couple exchanged vows with a city hall ceremony. “I had always pictured a classic courthouse skirt-suit look, but with a mini skirt,” Pam says. She tapped friend Nina Tiari to design it, and the two turned to Mugler’s structural jackets as a starting point for inspiration.
